CausalCCC step by step

From a raw count matrix to a causal network around ligand–receptor pairs: preprocessing, pitfalls, and how to choose the settings of each function

Author

Minh Le, Jeanne Leclerc

Published

October 14, 2026

Goal and running example

CausalCCC (Dupuis et al., NAR 2025) learns, with the causal network method MIIC, the intracellular genes linked to the ligands of sender cells and to the receptors of receiver cells. This tutorial goes through every step, says what to check at each one, and measures what each setting changes.

What CausalCCC is: MIIC, a data layout, and forced L-R links

CausalCCC is not a new network method: it is MIIC run on a specially built table, with the L-R pairs added as forced links. It has three parts:

Part What it does Where
1. Data preparation L-R pairs (causalCCC.links(), with LIANA), gene selection by mutual information (causalCCC.MIselection()), the table (causalCCC.mosaic()), the variable types (causalCCC.state_order()) R package causalCCC
2. The mosaic table sender and receiver cells stacked in one table; sender genes are NA in receiver cells and vice versa, so two genes of different cell types are never observed in the same cell the core idea of the method
3. A modified MIIC the L-R pairs are given as interact_edges: these links are forced (never removed, skeleton.cpp) and left out of the search for conditional independences; afterwards each gets the strength of the strongest link of the network miic, branch causalccc

Three consequences for reading a CausalCCC network:

  • The L-R links are imposed, not learnt. A ligand and its receptor are never measured in the same cells, so MIIC cannot estimate anything between them; their strength is set artificially (notebook case2/04, section 6).
  • What MIIC learns are the intracellular networks on each side: the genes linked to the ligand in the sender cells and to the receptor in the receiver cells. The forced L-R links are the bridge between them.
  • “Upstream” and “downstream” of an L-R pair mean a position relative to that link, not a causal direction found by MIIC across it (notebook case2/03).

The time-consuming parts are the gene selection (part 1) and, above all, the MIIC network reconstruction (part 3); notebook case2/10 makes both faster without changing their results.

The running example is case study 2 of the paper: fibroblasts, T cells and dendritic cells (DCs) from the skin of atopic dermatitis patients (He et al. 2020), with 43 ligand–receptor (L-R) pairs from CellChat. We use it because we know the answer: notebooks case2/03 to case2/09 rebuilt the authors’ input exactly, so every setting can be scored against the published one.

raw counts ─► QC, annotation ─► L-R pairs ─► gene selection (MI) ─► mosaic table + state order ─► MIIC ─► reading
 section 1      sections 2–3      section 4      section 5               sections 6–7                section 8   section 9

The package has six functions, all used below; the paper describes none of their settings in detail.

Function Role Section
causalCCC.links() L-R pairs with LIANA 4
causalCCC.MIselection() genes sharing the most mutual information (MI) with features of interest 5
causalCCC.mosaic() the cells × variables table, NA outside each cell type’s genes 6–7
causalCCC.state_order() type (discrete / continuous) and group of each variable 6–7
causalCCC.layout() drawing layout for the web server (cosmetic) 6
causalCCC.wrapper() all the above for one sender and one receiver population 6
miic() (package miic, branch causalccc) the causal network 8
NoteRunning time

First rendering: about 15 minutes for the gene selection (section 6) and about 50 minutes for the ten MIIC runs (section 8). Every result is saved in results/tutorial/ and reloaded afterwards; delete a file to recompute it. The full three-population network (section 7) takes 1 to 3 hours and is not run here (command given). Section 8b runs only when a web server job is given (-P server_job:<link>): a few minutes for a small network.

Setup

Three traps before starting:

  • miic must be attached before causalCCC. causalCCC.MIselection() calls miic() without importing it.
  • SeuratObject ≥ 5.3. causalCCC.MIselection() and causalCCC.mosaic() read the counts with GetAssayData(slot = "counts"), which is now an error (slot became layer). patch_causalccc_all() makes corrected copies of these two functions and of the wrapper, so that the wrapper calls the corrected copies. The installed package is not modified.
  • A bug of the wrapper with two or more metadata. causalCCC.MIselection() computes MI with every column of its table, metadata included, so a metadata column (here labels, which shares a lot of MI with condition) can come back among the selected “genes”. The wrapper then looks for it in the count matrix and stops with column not found: [labels], after the whole MI computation. The patched wrapper removes the metadata from the selected genes. When you call causalCCC.MIselection() yourself, do the same (setdiff(genes, metadata)).
library(tidyverse)
library(Matrix)
library(Seurat)
library(miic)
library(causalCCC)

root <- getwd()
while (!file.exists(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))) {
  if (dirname(root) == root) stop("Repository root not found. Open the repository folder in Positron.")
  root <- dirname(root)
}
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "helpers.R"))                       # select_genes(), link_name(), drawings ...
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "tutorial", "tutorial_helpers.R"))   # functions of this tutorial
source(file.path(root, "scripts", "benchmarks", "compare_outputs.R"))  # compare_miic(), section 8b

patch_causalccc_all()

# Server job to compare with (section 8b): the parameter when rendering, "" when the chunks are run by hand
server_job <- if (exists("params")) params$server_job else ""

job_dir     <- file.path(root, "data", "case2", "causalccc_server_w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa")   # the authors' files
results_dir <- file.path(root, "results", "tutorial")
dir.create(results_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)

cell_types <- c("Fibroblasts", "T_cell", "DCs")

Part 1 – Preparing the data

1. CausalCCC needs raw counts

Why. causalCCC.MIselection() and causalCCC.mosaic() read the counts layer, and MIIC computes mutual information on these values (it discretises continuous variables itself). Normalised, scaled, SCTransform or integrated values must not be used: they are not what the method was designed for, and log-normalisation introduces a dependence on library size that differs between genes.

Our data is CellChat’s data_humanSkin. Is it raw?

load(file.path(root, "data", "case2", "cellchat", "data_humanSkin_CellChat.rda"))
norm <- data_humanSkin$data
meta <- data_humanSkin$meta

dim(norm)
[1] 17328  7563
summary(norm@x)                         # non-zero values
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
 0.3059  1.5676  2.0859  2.1858  2.7000  8.1592 
all(norm@x == round(norm@x))            # whole numbers?
[1] FALSE

No: the values are log(1 + 10,000 × count / library size). Check this on any dataset before going further.

Recovering counts. In each cell, the smallest non-zero value is almost surely a count of 1. That gives the library size, then every count. recover_counts() does it (method of notebook case2/05).

counts <- recover_counts(norm, scale = 1e4)
attr(counts, "max_rounding_error")      # distance to the nearest whole number before rounding
[1] 3.410605e-12
summary(colSums(counts))                # library sizes
   Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
  103.0   482.5   923.0  1441.5  1839.0 27941.0

The values become whole numbers to within rounding noise, so the normalisation is exactly undone. This only works if (1) the scale factor is known (1e4 for Seurat and CellChat, 1e5 in some atlases, for example the thymus atlas of Park et al. 2020), (2) all the genes used for the normalisation are still in the matrix, and (3) the values were not scaled, regressed or integrated. Check that the maximum rounding error is tiny; if it is not, the counts cannot be recovered and the raw matrix must be found (GEO, the authors, or re-quantification from FASTQ files).

TipStarting from a real raw matrix (10x, kallisto|bustools, AnnData)

The skeleton below (not run) keeps the raw counts untouched while normalising only for clustering and annotation.

# 10x / kallisto|bustools output
raw <- Read10X("path/to/filtered_feature_bc_matrix")
so  <- CreateSeuratObject(raw, min.cells = 3, min.features = 200)
# ... QC (section 2), doublets, then:
so <- NormalizeData(so) |> FindVariableFeatures() |> ScaleData() |> RunPCA()   # for clustering only
# After IntegrateLayers() (Seurat 5), counts are split into one layer per sample: join them before CausalCCC,
# otherwise GetAssayData(layer = "counts") does not return all cells.
so <- JoinLayers(so)
# AnnData from scanpy: keep adata.layers["counts"] = adata.X.copy() BEFORE normalize_total(), and export that layer.

Gene names. CausalCCC matches L-R genes to the row names of the count matrix by exact name, and drops silently those it does not find (section 4). Check for duplicated names, make.unique() suffixes (.1), and that the matrix and the L-R resource use the same annotation: in case study 1, four genes had been renamed between annotations (for example Gnb2l1 → Rack1), and our kallisto run of case study 2 had ATP5F1E instead of ATP5E.

c(genes = nrow(counts),
  duplicated_names = sum(duplicated(rownames(counts))),
  make_unique_suffix = sum(str_detect(rownames(counts), "\\.[0-9]+$")))
             genes   duplicated_names make_unique_suffix 
             17328                  0                  7 
str_subset(rownames(counts), "\\.[0-9]+$")
[1] "CH17-340M24.3" "CTC-338M12.4"  "CTD-2201I18.1" "GS1-124K5.11" 
[5] "GS1-259H13.2"  "CTD-3080P12.3" "CTB-178M22.2"

Names ending in .1, .2… are either genuine names or the trace of make.unique() applied to duplicated symbols, in which case two genes shared one symbol upstream. Here all seven are genuine clone-based lncRNA names (such as CTD-2201I18.1), and none is an L-R gene.

2. Quality control on raw counts

CausalCCC has no QC of its own: every cell of the selected types enters the network. Cells that are empty droplets, doublets or damaged add spurious dependencies (a doublet expresses the genes of two cell types).

meta$cell_type <- recode(as.character(meta$labels),
  "APOE+ FIB" = "Fibroblasts", "FBN1+ FIB" = "Fibroblasts", "COL11A1+ FIB" = "Fibroblasts", "Inflam. FIB" = "Fibroblasts",
  "TC" = "T_cell", "Inflam. TC" = "T_cell", "CD40LG+ TC" = "T_cell", "NKT" = "T_cell",
  "cDC1" = "DCs", "cDC2" = "DCs", "LC" = "DCs", "Inflam. DC" = "DCs")
meta$labels <- as.character(meta$labels)

so <- CreateSeuratObject(counts = counts, meta.data = meta)

# Are the mitochondrial and ribosomal genes in the matrix?
c(mitochondrial_genes = sum(str_detect(rownames(so), "^MT-")), ribosomal_genes = sum(str_detect(rownames(so), "^RP[SL]")))
mitochondrial_genes     ribosomal_genes 
                  0                   0 
so@meta.data |>
  group_by(cell_type) |>
  summarise(cells = n(),
            median_counts = median(nCount_RNA), min_counts = min(nCount_RNA),
            median_genes = median(nFeature_RNA), min_genes = min(nFeature_RNA), max_genes = max(nFeature_RNA)) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 1)
cell_type cells median_counts min_counts median_genes min_genes max_genes
DCs 629 3015.0 185 1299.0 150 4523
Fibroblasts 4734 953.5 103 645.5 99 4238
T_cell 2200 698.0 104 493.0 98 2924 
so@meta.data |>
  select(cell_type, nCount_RNA, nFeature_RNA) |>
  pivot_longer(-cell_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(cell_type, value, fill = cell_type)) +
  geom_violin(scale = "width", show.legend = FALSE) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cell_type_colours) +
  facet_wrap(~name, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(x = NULL, y = NULL) +
  theme_minimal()

The matrix has no mitochondrial and no ribosomal genes: they were removed before CellChat normalised the data, so the library sizes recovered in section 1 exclude them. The mitochondrial filter cannot be checked on this dataset, and a PercentageFeatureSet(pattern = "^MT-") of 0 would mean missing genes, not healthy cells. Check that these genes are present before computing QC metrics.

This dataset was already filtered by its authors, so we only look. On a new dataset, typical filters are:

Filter Typical threshold Our kallisto run of case study 2 Comment
genes per cell > 200 (empty droplets) 200 < genes < 6,000 Park 2020: > 500 genes and > 2,000 counts
upper bound on genes or counts > 6,000–7,000 genes removed 6,000 a crude doublet filter
mitochondrial % < 5–20 %, tissue dependent < 15 % (skin) dissociated tissues tolerate more
doublets Scrublet (Python) or scDblFinder (R), per sample Scrublet not installed here, so not run
genes detected in ≥ 3 cells 3

Set the thresholds per cell type when the types differ a lot in size (DCs have about four times the counts of T cells here), and filter before recovering or storing the counts layer that CausalCCC will read.

Detection of the L-R genes. MI needs variation: a gene detected in a handful of cells carries almost no information, and its links will rest on few cells. Check the fraction of cells expressing each ligand and receptor in its own cell type.

lr_pairs <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "clean_interact_edges.tsv"),
                     col_names = c("ligand", "receptor"), show_col_types = FALSE)
split_var <- function(v) tibble(variable = v, gene = str_remove(v, "_(Fibroblasts|T_cell|DCs)$"),
                                cell_type = str_extract(v, "(Fibroblasts|T_cell|DCs)$"))
lr_roles <- bind_rows(split_var(lr_pairs$ligand) |> mutate(role = "ligand"),
                      split_var(lr_pairs$receptor) |> mutate(role = "receptor")) |>
  distinct()

detection <- lr_roles |>
  mutate(detected_in = map2_dbl(gene, cell_type, \(g, t) mean(counts[g, meta$cell_type == t] > 0))) |>
  arrange(detected_in)
detection |> mutate(detected_in = scales::percent(detected_in, 1)) |> head(10)
# A tibble: 10 × 5
   variable             gene     cell_type   role     detected_in
   <chr>                <chr>    <chr>       <chr>    <chr>      
 1 CCL19_Fibroblasts    CCL19    Fibroblasts ligand   6%         
 2 CD74_Fibroblasts     CD74     Fibroblasts receptor 8%         
 3 CCR7_DCs             CCR7     DCs         receptor 13%        
 4 IGFBP3_Fibroblasts   IGFBP3   Fibroblasts ligand   14%        
 5 IL13_T_cell          IL13     T_cell      ligand   15%        
 6 ACKR3_Fibroblasts    ACKR3    Fibroblasts receptor 15%        
 7 P4HB_T_cell          P4HB     T_cell      receptor 18%        
 8 BSG_T_cell           BSG      T_cell      receptor 19%        
 9 TNFSF14_T_cell       TNFSF14  T_cell      ligand   19%        
10 TNFRSF1A_Fibroblasts TNFRSF1A Fibroblasts receptor 22%

2 of the 44 L-R genes are detected in fewer than 10 % of the cells of their type (for example CCL19 in fibroblasts). They are kept because the L-R pair needs them, but links around them deserve caution. In fibroblasts, CCL19 is detected in 283 cells.

Ribosomal and mitochondrial genes. They are highly expressed in every cell and follow library size, so they share MI with almost any gene and invade the selection. In case study 1 the default selection contained 33 ribosomal genes, none of which the authors kept (notebook case1/03); removing them before the selection was needed to reproduce the authors’ input (notebook case1/04). This dataset has none, so the question does not arise here. On your data, count them among the best-ranked genes of the MI tables (section 5) and decide before the selection.

3. Populations and metadata

interact_ident is the metadata column that names the populations; senders and receivers are levels of it. Two properties of the populations matter.

Size. MIIC needs enough cells to detect dependencies: with few cells, only strong links survive. The paper’s smallest population has 151 cells (case study 3). Here:

table(meta$cell_type, meta$condition)
             
                LS   NL
  DCs          563   66
  Fibroblasts 2706 2028
  T_cell      1742  458

Confounders. Cells were pooled across conditions (LS = lesional, NL = non-lesional) and subtypes. Genes that differ between conditions or subtypes are then dependent through them; giving the condition and the subtype to MIIC as metadata variables lets it explain those dependencies instead of linking genes directly. The DCs are 90 % lesional, so in DCs the condition is nearly constant and carries little information; this also means DC links mostly describe lesional skin. When a metadata column is almost confounded with the cell type (for example the developmental stages of the thymus atlas), it cannot be separated from it.

Library size. Raw counts of most genes increase with the number of counts of the cell. That shared factor creates dependencies between genes that are not regulation. MIIC does not correct for it. We measure it on the genes the authors selected for DCs:

authors_mosaic <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "input.tsv"), guess_max = Inf, show_col_types = FALSE)
row_type <- case_when(!is.na(authors_mosaic$labels_Fibroblasts) ~ "Fibroblasts",
                      !is.na(authors_mosaic$labels_T_cell)      ~ "T_cell",
                      !is.na(authors_mosaic$labels_DCs)         ~ "DCs")
col_type <- column_cell_type(authors_mosaic, row_type)
strip    <- function(v) str_remove_all(v, "_(Fibroblasts|T_cell|DCs)")

# The authors' genes of each cell type (without metadata, suffixes and duplicated copies)
authors_genes <- map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) {
  unique(strip(names(authors_mosaic)[col_type == t & !str_detect(names(authors_mosaic), "^(labels|condition)_")]))
})

dc_cells <- which(meta$cell_type == "DCs")
cor_with_depth <- map_dbl(authors_genes$DCs, \(g) cor(counts[g, dc_cells], so$nCount_RNA[dc_cells], method = "spearman"))
summary(cor_with_depth)
    Min.  1st Qu.   Median     Mean  3rd Qu.     Max. 
-0.02677  0.45924  0.72060  0.62481  0.80814  0.89826

Most selected genes correlate positively with library size (median Spearman correlation 0.72). The published analyses do not correct for it. A possible safeguard, not used by the authors, is to add a discretised library size (for example its tertiles) as a metadata variable, so that MIIC can use it as a common cause.

4. Ligand–receptor pairs

CausalCCC does not infer communication itself: it takes L-R pairs as given. Two options:

  1. causalCCC.links(), which calls LIANA on the Seurat object (not run here, because the case study used CellChat):
causalCCC.links(so, species = "human", assay_name = "RNA", interact_ident = "cell_type",
                senders = "Fibroblasts", receivers = "DCs",
                CCC_method = "cellphonedb",  # or connectome, logfc, natmi, sca
                n_CCClinks = 30)             # pairs kept, ranked by the method's score
Argument Effect Advice
CCC_method ranking score: lr.mean (cellphonedb), prod_weight (natmi), LRscore (sca), weight_sc (connectome), logfc_comb (logfc) only cellphonedb and natmi also filter on p ≤ 0.05; the other three keep the top pairs whatever their significance
n_CCClinks number of pairs kept (default 30 here, 20 when called through the wrapper) each extra ligand or receptor adds MI computations (about one minute each) and genes to the network
species "mouse" converts the resource to mouse orthologues failed inside OmnipathR for case study 1 (mouse); give the pairs yourself then
  1. Your own pairs (CellChat, CellPhoneDB, NicheNet…), as a data frame with columns ligands and receptors.

Checks before using them:

  • Gene names. The wrapper keeps only the ligands and receptors found in the row names of the count matrix, without a warning. Complexes must be split into their subunits (the wrapper does it for LIANA receptors, separated by _, but not for ligands).
  • One table per direction. The wrapper handles one sender and one receiver. Here the 43 pairs span six directions:
directions <- lr_pairs |>
  transmute(sender = str_extract(ligand, "(Fibroblasts|T_cell|DCs)$"),
            receiver = str_extract(receptor, "(Fibroblasts|T_cell|DCs)$"),
            ligand = strip(ligand), receptor = strip(receptor))

directions |>
  group_by(sender, receiver) |>
  summarise(pairs = n(), ligands = n_distinct(ligand), receptors = n_distinct(receptor),
            receptor_order = paste(unique(receptor), collapse = " "), .groups = "drop")
# A tibble: 6 × 6
  sender      receiver    pairs ligands receptors receptor_order                
  <chr>       <chr>       <int>   <int>     <int> <chr>                         
1 DCs         Fibroblasts     6       5         6 ACKR3 BSG CD44 TNFRSF1A P4HB …
2 DCs         T_cell          7       3         6 CD74 CD44 CXCR4 BSG PTPRC P4HB
3 Fibroblasts DCs            11       7        10 CD74 CD44 CXCR4 FPR3 ITGAX IT…
4 Fibroblasts T_cell          5       3         4 CD74 CD44 CXCR4 BSG           
5 T_cell      DCs             9       6         9 CD74 CD44 CXCR4 FPR3 BSG IL13…
6 T_cell      Fibroblasts     5       3         5 CD74 CD44 ACKR3 BSG TNFRSF1A  
# Every L-R gene is in the matrix
all(c(directions$ligand, directions$receptor) %in% rownames(counts))
[1] TRUE

Note the order of the receptors: the wrapper uses only the first 8 ligands and the first 8 receptors of a direction as features of interest (section 5). Fibroblasts → DCs and T cells → DCs have more than 8 receptors.

Part 2 – Choosing the genes

5. Gene selection: causalCCC.MIselection()

What it computes

For one population (oneinteract), with a list of features of interest (goi, the ligands or receptors, plus the metadata of metadata_list):

  1. MI between each feature of interest and every gene of the matrix, computed by miic() without orientation, in blocks of 100 genes (the info_shifted value of each pair). A variable with 5 or fewer distinct values is treated as discrete. At most 30 features of interest. n_threads = 8 is fixed inside the function.
  2. The 3 genes with the highest MI with each feature of interest.
  3. The n_genes genes with the highest MI with any feature of interest. Default: max(15, min(4 × length(goi), 100)).
  4. Only genes with MI above bit_thresold (sic, default 0.001).

Step 1 takes about a minute per feature of interest; steps 2–4 are instant. So the efficient way to explore settings is to compute the MI table once (return_full = TRUE, or save = TRUE which writes <population>_MI_table.csv) and redo steps 2–4, which select_genes() (in scripts/helpers.R) reproduces line by line.

To compute the MI table itself, compute_mi_table() (scripts/helpers.R) gives exactly the table of causalCCC.MIselection(return_full = TRUE), about 20 % faster and with a third of the memory: it keeps the counts sparse and skips genes never detected in the population (notebook case2/10). Keep its blocks at about 100 genes (block_size, the package’s value): larger blocks are slower.

One subtlety: the MI table contains a row for every column of the population’s table, metadata included. The MI tables reused here were computed with both metadata, so labels is a candidate “gene” in them; in a call with condition only, it is not. We check select_genes() on one small call, removing labels from the candidates to match it:

# MI tables of every gene with every ligand, receptor and metadata of each cell type (notebook case2/05, 30 minutes)
mi_tables <- readRDS(file.path(root, "results", "case2", "05_rebuild_input", "mi_tables.rds"))

check_file <- file.path(results_dir, "miselection_check.rds")
if (!file.exists(check_file)) {
  invisible(capture.output(suppressMessages(
    package_genes <- causalCCC.MIselection(so, assay_name = "RNA", interact_ident = "cell_type", oneinteract = "DCs",
                                           goi = "CXCR4", metadata_list = "condition"))))
  saveRDS(package_genes, check_file)
}
package_genes <- readRDS(check_file)

our_genes <- select_genes(filter(mi_tables, cell_type == "DCs", variables != "labels"), foi = c("CXCR4", "condition"),
                          n_genes = default_n_genes("CXCR4"))
identical(package_genes, our_genes)
[1] TRUE
package_genes
 [1] "RGS1"     "NR4A3"    "GPR183"   "HLA-DQA2" "EIF2AK4"  "CAMSAP2" 
 [7] "CD83"     "BTG1"     "EIF1"     "UBC"      "PTGER4"   "DUSP4"   
[13] "ID2"      "SAT1"     "SRGN"     "HERPUD1"  "REL"      "CDKN1A"  
# With labels left among the candidates, it is selected as if it were a gene
setdiff(select_genes(filter(mi_tables, cell_type == "DCs"), foi = c("CXCR4", "condition"), n_genes = 15), package_genes)
[1] "labels"

This is the origin of the wrapper bug patched in the Setup: a metadata column selected as a gene. Always remove the metadata from the selected genes (setdiff(genes, metadata)).

How many genes? (n_genes)

The MI of the best genes falls quickly, then flattens. The curve of each feature of interest shows where the informative genes end:

mi_tables |>
  filter(cell_type == "DCs", foi %in% c("CXCR4", "CD74", "CCR7", "ITGAX", "labels", "condition")) |>
  group_by(foi) |>
  slice_max(value, n = 100, with_ties = FALSE) |>
  mutate(rank = row_number()) |>
  ggplot(aes(rank, value, colour = foi)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 25, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  labs(x = "rank of the gene", y = "MI with the feature of interest (info_shifted)", colour = "feature",
       title = "DCs: MI of the 100 best genes of each feature of interest") +
  theme_minimal()

The subtype labels shares more MI with genes than most ligands and receptors (it ranks 3rd or 4th in each cell type, behind highly expressed genes such as CD74, MIF or PPIA): as a feature of interest, it pulls in subtype markers. condition shares little MI with any gene (it ranks near the bottom in each cell type). The selection takes the top n_genes by their highest MI over all features, so it is dominated by the features with the largest MI.

Scoring the settings

We now vary one setting at a time, in the protocol that reproduces the authors’ input exactly (notebook case2/07): one selection per sender → receiver direction, pooled per cell type. Each setting is scored against the authors’ selected genes (L-R genes excluded, since they are always kept): missing = authors’ genes not selected, extra = genes selected but not used by the authors.

lr_genes  <- map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) lr_roles$gene[lr_roles$cell_type == t])
both_meta <- c("labels", "condition")
fixed     <- function(n) \(goi) n

settings <- tribble(
  ~setting,                                ~meta_s,     ~meta_r,     ~cap, ~n_genes,            ~drop,
  "exact (authors): 25 genes, no cap, both metadata", both_meta, both_meta, Inf, list(fixed(25)), NA,
  "n_genes = 15",                          both_meta,   both_meta,   Inf,  list(fixed(15)),     NA,
  "n_genes = 50",                          both_meta,   both_meta,   Inf,  list(fixed(50)),     NA,
  "n_genes = 100",                         both_meta,   both_meta,   Inf,  list(fixed(100)),    NA,
  "n_genes = default formula",             both_meta,   both_meta,   Inf,  list(default_n_genes), NA,
  "cap of 8 (wrapper)",                    both_meta,   both_meta,   8,    list(fixed(25)),     NA,
  "no metadata",                           NULL,        NULL,        Inf,  list(fixed(25)),     NA,
  "labels only",                           "labels",    "labels",    Inf,  list(fixed(25)),     NA,
  "condition only",                        "condition", "condition", Inf,  list(fixed(25)),     NA,
  "ribosomal + mitochondrial removed",     both_meta,   both_meta,   Inf,  list(fixed(25)),     "^(RP[SL]|MT-)",
  "wrapper defaults (cap 8, default n_genes)", both_meta, both_meta, 8,    list(default_n_genes), NA)

selections <- pmap(settings, \(setting, meta_s, meta_r, cap, n_genes, drop) {
  if (!is.function(n_genes)) n_genes <- n_genes[[1]]   # tribble() keeps the function inside a list
  select_by_direction(mi_tables, directions, meta_s, meta_r, cap = cap, n_genes = n_genes,
                      drop = if (is.na(drop)) NULL else drop)
}) |> set_names(settings$setting)

authors_selected <- map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) setdiff(authors_genes[[t]], lr_genes[[t]]))

One selection per direction or per cell type? The alternative is a single selection per cell type with all its ligands and receptors together:

per_cell_type <- map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) {
  goi <- unique(lr_genes[[t]])
  setdiff(select_genes(filter(mi_tables, cell_type == t), foi = c(goi, both_meta), n_genes = 25), both_meta)
})

What to retain

  • n_genes is the main size knob. Below 25, the authors’ genes go missing; above, genes are added quickly (50 genes per run nearly doubles the network with no gain). Every gene costs MIIC time and adds weaker candidates. With 3 to 10 genes of interest per run here, the default formula gives 15 to 40 genes per run. Pick n_genes from the MI curves (where they flatten) and from the network size MIIC can handle (about 200 variables in 1–3 hours on one thread; 51 variables in about 4 minutes, section 8).
  • The cap of 8 is silent. With more than 8 ligands or receptors in a direction, the extra ones get no selected genes of their own: their top genes (for example those of TMEM219 and TNFRSF14 in DCs) disappear. Their order in the L-R table decides which are dropped. Call causalCCC.MIselection() directly to avoid it (at most 30 features).
  • Metadata as features of interest change the selection (they bring subtype and condition markers). Without them, about a fifth of the authors’ genes are lost; labels carries most of the effect, condition adds a few genes. Keeping them is what the authors did; it makes the network describe subtype structure as well as signalling.
  • One selection per direction, not per cell type. A single selection per cell type with all its ligands and receptors keeps fewer genes per L-R gene, and loses up to 18 of the authors’ genes in fibroblasts.
  • Removing ribosomal and mitochondrial genes changes nothing here, because the matrix has none (section 2); in case study 1 it was essential.
  • bit_thresold only removes genes with essentially no MI; it never mattered in our tests.

6. The wrapper, causalCCC.wrapper(), on one direction

The wrapper chains sections 4 and 5 and builds the files for MIIC, for one sender and one receiver. Its arguments:

Argument Default What it does Advice
data_input Seurat object with the raw counts in assay_name (the documentation also allows a data frame) use a Seurat object (CreateSeuratObject(counts, meta.data = meta)): the data-frame path is broken, the wrapper looks for the L-R genes in row.names(data_input), which are cell names, so it drops every pair (notebook case2/05)
interact_ident, senders_name, receivers_name NULL population column and levels always give all three (otherwise the first two levels of the active identity are taken)
do_CCC, CCC_method, n_CCClinks FALSE, cellphonedb, 20 run causalCCC.links() (section 4); do_CCC = TRUE forces do_MIselect = TRUE cellphonedb is used only with do_CCC = TRUE; by default no pair is inferred and interact_edges must be given (as below)
interact_edges NULL data frame with columns ligands, receptors required if do_CCC = FALSE; order matters (cap of 8)
do_MIselect FALSE run the MI selection otherwise give genes_senders and genes_receivers
n_genes_senders, n_genes_receivers NULL = default formula n_genes of each selection (≤ 500) section 5
goi_senders, goi_receivers NULL extra features of interest (a transcription factor, a marker…): genes are selected around them as around the ligands / receptors; they are added before the first 8 ligands / receptors each one takes a place among the 8
metadata_senders, metadata_receivers list() named list: names = metadata columns, values = their levels in increasing order (written to the state order). The metadata are features of interest of the selection (they pull in their markers) and nodes of the network (a dependence due to the condition or the subtype goes through them instead of a direct gene–gene link, section 3) a character vector is not accepted by causalCCC.state_order()
genes_senders, genes_receivers NULL genes added to the selection, or the full lists if do_MIselect = FALSE
save, plot TRUE MI tables and heatmaps in wd_path/MI_tables/ keep save = TRUE: the tables let you redo the selection with other settings in seconds
do_layout, wd_path FALSE, working dir layout for the web server; output folder CausalCCC_files/

Hidden behaviours to know: the cap of 8; with two metadata or more it stops after the MI computation unless patched (see Setup); ligands and receptors missing from the matrix are dropped silently; a gene selected in both the sender and the receiver population of the run (for example B2M in fibroblasts and in DCs) is written as two columns, B2M_senders and B2M_receivers, while a gene selected on one side only keeps its plain name; metadata given on both sides are suffixed the same way; cells are shuffled with sample(), so set a seed.

We run it on fibroblasts → DCs, the direction of CXCL12–CXCR4 (Figure 3 of the paper), with the default settings and both metadata.

pairs_fib_dc <- directions |> filter(sender == "Fibroblasts", receiver == "DCs") |>
  transmute(ligands = ligand, receptors = receptor) |> as.data.frame()
levels_of <- function(t) list(labels = sort(unique(meta$labels[meta$cell_type == t])), condition = c("NL", "LS"))

wrapper_dir  <- file.path(results_dir, "wrapper_fibroblasts_dcs")
wrapper_file <- file.path(wrapper_dir, "wrapper_output.rds")

  set.seed(2026)
  invisible(capture.output(suppressMessages(
    wrapper_out <- causalCCC.wrapper(so, assay_name = "RNA", interact_ident = "cell_type",
                                     senders_name = "Fibroblasts", receivers_name = "DCs",
                                     interact_edges = pairs_fib_dc, do_MIselect = TRUE,
                                     metadata_senders = levels_of("Fibroblasts"),
                                     metadata_receivers = levels_of("DCs"),
                                     save = TRUE, plot = TRUE, wd_path = wrapper_dir))))
  saveRDS(wrapper_out, wrapper_file)
}

7. Mosaic table and state order, for more than two populations

The mosaic table

One row per cell, one column per variable; a sender gene is NA in receiver cells and the reverse. MIIC uses, for each pair of variables, the cells where both are observed: two genes of different populations are never observed together, so they can only be linked through the L-R pairs given in interact_edges.

mosaic_w <- wrapper_out$mosaic_table
is_sender_row <- !is.na(mosaic_w$labels_senders)
# a ligand and a receptor, with the names the wrapper gave them
ligand_col   <- str_subset(wrapper_out$interact_edges$ligands, "^CXCL12")[1]
receptor_col <- str_subset(wrapper_out$interact_edges$receptors, "^CXCR4")[1]
tibble(rows = c("sender cells", "receiver cells"),
       n = c(sum(is_sender_row), sum(!is_sender_row)),
       !!paste(ligand_col, "observed")   := c(mean(!is.na(mosaic_w[[ligand_col]][is_sender_row])),
                                              mean(!is.na(mosaic_w[[ligand_col]][!is_sender_row]))),
       !!paste(receptor_col, "observed") := c(mean(!is.na(mosaic_w[[receptor_col]][is_sender_row])),
                                              mean(!is.na(mosaic_w[[receptor_col]][!is_sender_row]))))

  rows               n `CXCL12 observed` `CXCR4 observed`

1 sender cells    4734                 1                0
2 receiver cells   629                 0                1

The state order and the discrete rule

causalCCC.state_order() declares a variable discrete if it has 5 or fewer distinct values, counting NA. In a mosaic table every gene has NA in the other population, so a gene with 4 or fewer observed values (mostly 0) becomes discrete. This decides how MIIC treats it. To estimate MI with a continuous variable, MIIC cuts its values into intervals, choosing the number and the bounds of the intervals itself (not necessarily two, and not 0/1 by design). A discrete variable is not cut: each of its values (0, 1, 2, 3…) is a category of its own. Here:

wrapper_out$state_order |>
  filter(var_type == 0, group != "metadata") |>
  mutate(observed_values = map_chr(var_names, \(v) paste(sort(unique(na.omit(mosaic_w[[v]]))), collapse = ",")))
[1] var_names               var_type                levels_increasing_order
[4] is_contextual           group                   group_color            
[7] observed_values        
<0 rows> (or 0-length row.names)

No gene is discrete in this direction: the selected genes are well expressed. The rule matters for rare genes: in case study 1, Tgfb1 was discrete on the sender side only (notebook case1/02). Apply the same rule when you build the table yourself (as below), otherwise the network changes.

Several directions

The case study has six directions. Running the wrapper six times and pooling the tables by column name is how the authors’ input was probably built, and the most likely origin of its 14 duplicated columns (notebook case2/05, section 10). In one run, a gene selected in both populations gets a suffix and otherwise keeps its plain name, so the same gene of the same cell type can be suffixed in one run and plain in another. With the authors’ selection, S100A6 of fibroblasts is plain in the two directions with DCs, but suffixed in the two directions with T cells, which select it too. The authors’ table holds two identical copies of it, S100A6_Fibroblasts and S100A6_Fibroblasts_Fibroblasts. All 14 duplicated genes are in this situation, but so are 25 genes that are not duplicated: the naming explains which genes can be duplicated, not exactly which ones are. The name also depends on the settings: with the wrapper’s defaults (section 6), S100A6 is suffixed in fibroblasts → DCs too. Each of the 14 duplicates is one gene of one cell type under two names that differ only in the number of cell-type suffixes: 9 are GENE_T = GENE_T_T (as S100A6), 5 are GENE = GENE_T. Duplicates do not change the gene–gene links, but the two copies of a gene get contradictory orientations (87 of their 111 links), and the strength given to all L-R links is set by the duplicate pair (11,579 instead of 3,050; notebook case2/09). With several threads and the unpatched miic, they also make the orientations depend on the timing of the threads (notebook case2/10). Check for identical columns before running MIIC (duplicated_columns(), below).

The safe way: select the genes per direction, pool them per cell type, and name every variable <gene>_<cell type>. build_mosaic() and build_state_order() do that with the rules of the package.

exact <- selections[["exact (authors): 25 genes, no cap, both metadata"]]
genes_per_type <- map(set_names(cell_types), \(t) unique(c(lr_genes[[t]], exact[[t]])))
lengths(genes_per_type)

# Checks before MIIC

The table has the authors’ genes, each once (the authors’ table has 238 columns: these 224 variables plus their 14 duplicates). The three files are written in the server’s format; MIIC on them takes 1–3 hours on one thread, and about 3 times less on 8 threads with the patched miic variant deterministic (docs/INSTALL.md, section 4; on case study 2, 70 → 22 minutes, and 91 → 30 minutes on the authors’ input, with the one-thread links, orientations and genuine causations; only the confidence values move slightly, notebook case2/10). The installed miic crashes with more than one thread.

  results/tutorial/three_populations 8

Part 3 – The causal network

8. MIIC settings, on a small network

To compare MIIC settings in minutes, we build a small network around CXCL12–CXCR4: fibroblasts → DCs, the ligands CXCL12 and MIF, the receptors CXCR4, CD74 and CD44, and 12 genes per side selected from the wrapper’s MI tables. We call the wrapper again with do_MIselect = FALSE and our gene lists (no MI computation).

pairs_small <- data.frame(ligands   = c("MIF", "MIF", "MIF", "CXCL12"),
                          receptors = c("CD74", "CD44", "CXCR4", "CXCR4"))
small_genes <- list(
  senders   = setdiff(select_genes(wrapper_mi$Fibroblasts, c("CXCL12", "MIF", both_meta), n_genes = 12), both_meta),
  receivers = setdiff(select_genes(wrapper_mi$DCs, c("CXCR4", "CD74", "CD44", both_meta), n_genes = 12), both_meta))

small_dir <- file.path(results_dir, "small_network")
dir.create(small_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
set.seed(2026)
invisible(capture.output(suppressMessages(
  small <- causalCCC.wrapper(so, assay_name = "RNA", interact_ident = "cell_type",
                             senders_name = "Fibroblasts", receivers_name = "DCs",
                             interact_edges = pairs_small, do_MIselect = FALSE,
                             genes_senders = small_genes$senders, genes_receivers = small_genes$receivers,
                             metadata_senders = levels_of("Fibroblasts"), metadata_receivers = levels_of("DCs"),
                             wd_path = small_dir))))

# miic() reads interact_edges$ligand and interact_edges$receptor: rename the wrapper's columns
small_edges <- small$interact_edges |> transmute(ligand = ligands, receptor = receptors)
dim(small$mosaic_table)
[1] 5363   51
small_edges
  ligand receptor
1    MIF     CD74

4 CXCL12    CXCR4
WarningColumn names of interact_edges

miic() reads interact_edges$ligand and interact_edges$receptor. The wrapper writes ligands / receptors (which still works through R’s partial matching of $, with a warning); any other names (from/to, l/r) make the run fail at the very end, after the whole computation.

The settings

The authors’ server jobs ran MIIC with settings that differ from miic()’s defaults on three points (server job script.sh, notebooks case1/02 and case2/04). The last column is the field of the server’s submission form (workbench_causalCCC.php) that sets each one, with its default value:

miic() argument Default Authors’ server job Meaning Server form field (default)
ori_proba_ratio 1 0.01 an arrowhead is kept only if its probability is above 1/(1 + ratio): 0.5 by default, 0.99 on the server orientation probability ratio (1)
n_shuffles 0 100 number of permutations to measure the confidence of each link confidence cut (no), number of shuffles (100)
conf_threshold 0 0.01 links whose confidence ratio is above this are removed (needs n_shuffles > 0) confidence threshold (0.01)
cplx "nml" "nml" complexity penalty: "nml" (normalised maximum likelihood) or "mdl" (minimum description length, close to BIC). Any other value (for example "bic") is replaced by the default with only a warning –
latent "orientation" "orientation" allow latent common causes when orienting (bidirected links <->); "no" forbids them, "yes" also uses them when removing links latent (orientation)
consistent "no" "no" "orientation" / "skeleton" iterate until separating sets are consistent with the graph (slower) consistency (no)
test_mar, n_eff TRUE, -1 same missing-at-random test for NA; effective number of samples (-1 = automatic) KL test (yes), effN (-1)
propagation, negative_info FALSE, FALSE same propagate the orientations along the network; allow negative conditional information when removing links propagation, negative info (no)
n_threads 1 1 keep 1 with the installed miic: 2 and 4 threads crashed with C stack errors on our inputs; 8 threads work with the patched variant (section 7) –
seed none none only the permutations are random seed (0)
ImportantThe server’s form defaults are not the authors’ settings

By default the form runs without the confidence cut and with an orientation probability ratio of 1: a job submitted with the defaults is comparable with miic()‘s defaults, not with the published networks. To reproduce the authors’ settings, set confidence cut = yes, 100 shuffles, confidence threshold 0.01, orientation probability ratio 0.01, and leave the rest by default. This is why our first server jobs of case study 1 (8 October) could not be compared with the authors’ network (data/README.md). Section 8b compares a server job with a local run.

We run the small network with the authors’ settings, then change one setting at a time. Two runs test what should not matter: another seed (other permutations), and another order of the cells (the mosaic is shuffled by sample()).

small_mosaic <- small$mosaic_table
small_state  <- small$state_order
run_file <- function(name) file.path(small_dir, paste0("miic_", name, ".rds"))
run <- function(name, mosaic = small_mosaic, seed = 2026, ...)
  run_miic_cached(run_file(name), mosaic, small_state, small_edges, seed = seed, ...)

set.seed(7)
shuffled_rows <- small_mosaic[sample(nrow(small_mosaic)), ]

runs <- list(
  "authors' settings (reference)"     = run("reference"),
  "miic() defaults"                    = run("defaults", ori_proba_ratio = 1, n_shuffles = 0, conf_threshold = 0),
  "no confidence filter"               = run("no_shuffles", n_shuffles = 0, conf_threshold = 0),
  "ori_proba_ratio = 1"                = run("ori_ratio_1", ori_proba_ratio = 1),
  "latent = no"                        = run("latent_no", latent = "no"),
  "cplx = mdl"                         = run("mdl", cplx = "mdl"),
  "consistent = orientation"           = run("consistent", consistent = "orientation"),
  "other seed"                         = run("seed_7", seed = 7),
  "other cell order"                   = run("rows_shuffled", mosaic = shuffled_rows))

compare_runs(runs, "authors' settings (reference)", small_edges) |>
  mutate(across(c(jaccard_links, same_orientation, same_causal), \(v) round(v, 2))) |>
  knitr::kable()
run minutes links not_oriented oriented bidirected genuine_causes jaccard_links same_orientation same_causal

miic() defaults 4.4 120 79 38 3 7 0.92 0.91 0.97
no confidence filter 4.1 120 89 28 3 3 0.92 0.98 1.00

latent = no 4.1 111 84 27 0 NA 1.00 0.95 NA
cplx = mdl 1.1 88 39 23 26 11 0.51 0.51 0.87
consistent = orientation 5.0 126 97 27 2 1 0.85 0.95 0.98
other seed 4.0 111 81 27 3 3 1.00 1.00 1.00

jaccard_links = shared links / links in either network; same_orientation and same_causal are computed on the links shared with the reference. L-R links are excluded (they are imposed).

genuine_causes is NA with latent = "no": this version of miic reports no genuine causation in that mode.

What changes the network, and what does not:

  • Seed and cell order: nothing. Another seed (other permutations) and another order of the cells give exactly the reference network. The random parts of the pipeline do not matter at this size; the settings do.
  • The confidence filter removes weak links. Without permutations (n_shuffles = 0), MIIC keeps 9 more links, all weak; the orientations of the shared links barely change.
  • ori_proba_ratio sets how many arrows are drawn. At 1 (the default, arrowhead probability > 0.5) more links are oriented and genuine causations nearly double; at 0.01 (the server, > 0.99) only the clearest arrows remain.
  • miic() with its defaults combines both effects: more links, more arrows, more than twice the genuine causations. A network run with the defaults (in R or with the server’s default form) is therefore not comparable with the published ones: always report these three settings.
  • latent = "no" turns the bidirected links (shared hidden causes) into ordinary ones and stops reporting genuine causation.
  • consistent = "orientation" changes the links most here (Jaccard 0.85) and keeps a single genuine causation: results obtained with and without it should not be mixed.
  • cplx = "mdl" changes the network most: it is four times faster, but it shares only half of the reference links and turns many links into bidirected ones. NML is the penalty CausalCCC was published with; keep it.
  • Invalid values are ignored. A first version of this run used cplx = "bic", which this version of miic does not know: it silently ran with "nml" and returned the reference network. run_miic_cached() now stops when the settings used differ from those requested; check result$params in your own runs.

Rule of thumb. Fix the settings before looking at the network, use the server’s (they are what the papers used), and treat any oriented link that depends on ori_proba_ratio as fragile.

Choosing conf_threshold and ori_proba_ratio from one run

conf_threshold has no upper bound in miic (R/miic.utils.R, l. 1109). One run with n_shuffles = 100 and conf_threshold = 1e10 therefore computes the confidence of every link and cuts none: the links that a threshold t would keep are those with a confidence ratio of at most t, which gives the exact curve of the links kept for every threshold. With ori_proba_ratio = 1 in the same run, the arrowhead probabilities (proba) of all links are kept, which gives the number of links oriented for every ratio (an arrowhead is drawn if its probability is above 1/(1 + ratio)). This curve is only approximate: the orientations are computed on the uncut network, which has more links than the network of any threshold.

As a reference we count, among the links kept, those of the published network (between the same genes of the same cell types; the authors’ network has many more variables, so it is not the answer for this small network).

uncut <- run("uncut", conf_threshold = 1e10, ori_proba_ratio = 1)
uncut_links <- retained_links(uncut, small_edges) |> filter(!is_lr)

# Names of the small network -> names of the authors' table (<gene>_<cell type>, one name per gene and cell type)
side_of <- set_names(if_else(small_state$group %in% c("ligands", "senders genes") |
                               str_detect(small_state$var_names, "_senders$"), "Fibroblasts", "DCs"),
                     small_state$var_names)
authors_name <- \(v) paste0(str_remove(v, "_(senders|receivers)$"), "_", side_of[v])
authors_norm <- set_names(paste0(strip(names(authors_mosaic)), "_", col_type), names(authors_mosaic))
paper_links  <- read_tsv(file.path(job_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt"), show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  filter(type == "P") |>
  transmute(link = link_name(authors_norm[x], authors_norm[y])) |>
  pull(link) |> unique()
in_paper <- link_name(authors_name(uncut_links$x), authors_name(uncut_links$y)) %in% paper_links

thresholds <- 10^seq(-4, 0, by = 0.02)
ratios     <- 10^seq(-3, 0, by = 0.02)
arrowhead  <- map_dbl(str_split(uncut_links$proba, ";"), \(p) max(as.numeric(p)))
curves <- bind_rows(
  tibble(panel = "confidence threshold (conf_threshold)", value = thresholds,
         `links kept`                       = map_int(thresholds, \(t) sum(uncut_links$confidence <= t, na.rm = TRUE)),
         `links kept, in the paper's network` = map_int(thresholds, \(t) sum(uncut_links$confidence <= t & in_paper, na.rm = TRUE))),
  tibble(panel = "orientation probability ratio (ori_proba_ratio), approximate", value = ratios,
         `links with an arrowhead` = map_int(ratios, \(r) sum(arrowhead > 1 / (1 + r))))) |>
  pivot_longer(-c(panel, value), names_to = "series", values_to = "links", values_drop_na = TRUE)

ggplot(curves, aes(value, links, colour = series)) +
  geom_step() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0.01, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey50") +
  scale_x_log10() +
  facet_wrap(~panel, scales = "free") +
  labs(x = "setting (log scale; dashed: the authors' value, 0.01)", y = "links (L-R links excluded)", colour = NULL) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
# Checks: the curves at the authors' values against the reference run (cut at 0.01, ratio 0.01)
ref_net <- retained_links(runs[["authors' settings (reference)"]], small_edges) |> filter(!is_lr)
tibble(quantity = c("links kept at conf_threshold = 0.01", "links with an arrowhead at ori_proba_ratio = 0.01",
                    "links with an arrowhead at ori_proba_ratio = 1"),
       curve = c(sum(uncut_links$confidence <= 0.01, na.rm = TRUE), sum(arrowhead > 1 / 1.01), sum(arrowhead > 0.5)),
       run   = c(nrow(ref_net), sum(ref_net$infOrt != 1), sum(uncut_links$infOrt != 1)),
       which_run = c("reference", "reference", "uncut")) |>
  knitr::kable()
quantity curve run which_run
links kept at conf_threshold = 0.01 111 111 reference
links with an arrowhead at ori_proba_ratio = 0.01 31 30 reference
links with an arrowhead at ori_proba_ratio = 1 41 41 uncut 
c(paper_links_between_these_variables = sum(map_lgl(str_split(paper_links, " \\| "), \(p)
    all(p %in% authors_name(small_state$var_names)) && p[1] != p[2])))
paper_links_between_these_variables 
                                 77

The confidence curve is exact: at 0.01 it gives the 111 links of the reference run. On this small network it has no sharp elbow: about 100 links are kept even at a threshold of 1e-4, and the next ones are added slowly, one by one, up to 120 at a threshold of 1. Of the 77 links of the paper’s network between these variables, 72 are already kept below a threshold of 0.003: the links added above it are not in the paper’s network, consistent with a confidence filter that removes weakly supported links. The orientation curve rises steadily: about 27 links with an arrowhead at a ratio of 0.001, 31 at 0.01 (30 in the reference run, hence “approximate”) and 41 at 1, the miic() and server default. Lowering the ratio is a choice of how sure an arrow must be; nothing in the curve singles out one value.

How to use these curves on your data. Look for the elbow: the threshold below which the number of links kept falls quickly (strong links only) and above which it rises slowly (links added one by one, each weakly supported). Do not pick the setting that recovers the most links of a published network: that reasoning is circular (the published network was itself obtained with one choice of settings), and it would hide the differences you are looking for. Fix the settings first, then compare.

8b. Comparing with a run on the web server

The CausalCCC web server runs the same MIIC. Comparing one of its jobs with a local run checks three things at once: that the settings are those you think, that the input is the same table, and that the network is the same. The job is a parameter of this notebook: paste its link (or its 20-character code) when rendering,

quarto render notebooks/tutorial/causalccc_tutorial.qmd -P server_job:https://miic.curie.fr/...<code>...

or, when running the chunks by hand in Positron, set server_job <- "<link or code>" in the console after the setup chunk. Without a job, the chunks of this section are skipped.

TipSubmitting a job to compare with
  1. Upload the three files the wrapper wrote for the small network of section 8, in results/tutorial/small_network/CausalCCC_files/: causalCCC_df.csv (the mosaic table), causalCCC_st.tsv (the state order) and causalCCC_interactEdges.tsv (the L-R pairs). It runs in a few minutes, on the server and here.
  2. In the form, set confidence cut = yes, number of shuffles = 100, confidence threshold = 0.01, orientation probability ratio = 0.01, and leave the rest by default (section 8: the form’s defaults are not the authors’ settings). Or keep the defaults on purpose, to see the comparison flag the difference.
  3. When the job is finished, copy the link of its result page (or of any of its files) and render with -P server_job:<link>.

The authors’ jobs work too: eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC (case study 1) and w0788tM1wzXGHLzNaKKa (case study 2, already in data/; its local run takes 1–3 hours, see below).

Downloading the job

The files of a job are at https://miic.curie.fr/server/server_outputs/<code>/<file>. We keep six of them in data/<case>/causalccc_server_<code>/ (case1 for the authors’ case 1 job, case2 otherwise), skip those already there and log each download in data/download_log.tsv, as the download scripts do.

server_code <- server_job_id(server_job)
server_case <- if (server_code == "eaP9Br0llvzxN07zZZEC") "case1" else "case2"
server_dir  <- file.path(root, "data", server_case, paste0("causalccc_server_", server_code))
download_server_job(server_code, server_dir, file.path(root, "data", "download_log.tsv"), root) |>
  knitr::kable()

needed <- c("script.sh", "edgesList.miic.summary.txt", "input.tsv", "clean_state_order.tsv", "clean_interact_edges.tsv")
if (!all(file.exists(file.path(server_dir, needed))))
  stop("Missing files for job ", server_code, ": ", paste(needed[!file.exists(file.path(server_dir, needed))],
       collapse = ", "), ". Is the job finished? Check its page on miic.curie.fr.")

1. Settings

script.sh holds the command the server ran. Each option is translated into the miic() argument it sets and compared with the settings of scripts/run_miic.R (the authors’ settings, authors_miic_settings). An option absent from the command gets the miic() default (an absent flag, such as --orientation, means FALSE).

server_parsed <- parse_server_script(file.path(server_dir, "script.sh"))
settings_table <- compare_settings(server_parsed, authors_miic_settings)
knitr::kable(settings_table)

# Options of the command that this notebook does not translate, as they are written
server_parsed |> filter(!known) |> select(option, written)

settings_differ <- any(settings_table$note == "DIFFERS")
settings_differ

2. Same input?

The server stores the table it received as input.tsv. We compare it with the tables of this tutorial (columns, then values); the closest one comes first.

server_input <- read_tsv(file.path(server_dir, "input.tsv"), guess_max = Inf, show_col_types = FALSE)
local_tables <- list("small network (section 8)"     = small_mosaic,
                     "fibroblasts → DCs (section 6)" = wrapper_out$mosaic_table,
                     "three populations (section 7)" = mosaic3,
                     "authors' input, case study 2"  = authors_mosaic)
imap(local_tables, \(t, name) compare_inputs(server_input, t) |> mutate(local_table = name, .before = 1)) |>
  list_rbind() |>
  arrange(desc(columns_shared / pmax(columns_server, columns_local))) |>
  knitr::kable()

3. Networks

The local run is scripts/run_miic.R on the server’s own three files, so that only MIIC is compared. It is run here for networks of up to 100 variables (a few minutes); for a larger one, the chunk prints the command to run in a terminal (1–3 hours on one thread, about 3 times less with the patched variant on 8 threads), and the comparison appears at the next rendering. If the settings differ (step 1), a second local run uses the server’s settings (saved as a list of miic() arguments, which run_miic.R accepts as its sixth argument): the difference between the two local runs is the effect of the settings, and the difference between the server and the second local run is the effect of the server.

server_runs_dir <- file.path(results_dir, paste0("server_", server_code))
server_result   <- list(all.edges.summary = read_tsv(file.path(server_dir, "edgesList.miic.summary.txt"),
                                                     show_col_types = FALSE))

local_run <- run_miic_script(root, server_dir, file.path(server_runs_dir, "local_settings"))
local_server_settings_run <- NULL
if (settings_differ) {
  settings_file <- file.path(server_runs_dir, "server_settings.rds")
  dir.create(server_runs_dir, recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
  saveRDS(server_settings_list(server_parsed), settings_file)
  local_server_settings_run <- run_miic_script(root, server_dir, file.path(server_runs_dir, "server_settings"),
                                               settings_file = settings_file)
}

comparisons <- list(
  "server vs local run, our settings"                = list(server_result, local_run),
  "server vs local run, server's settings"           = list(server_result, local_server_settings_run),
  "local runs: our settings vs the server's settings" = list(local_run, local_server_settings_run))
comparisons <- keep(comparisons, \(pair) !is.null(pair[[1]]) && !is.null(pair[[2]]))
if (length(comparisons) == 0) {
  cat("No local run yet: run the command printed above, then render again.\n")
} else {
  imap(comparisons, \(pair, name) compare_miic(pair[[1]], pair[[2]]) |> mutate(comparison = name, .before = 1)) |>
    list_rbind() |>
    mutate(across(where(is.double), \(v) signif(v, 3))) |>
    knitr::kable()
}

How to read the verdict (compare_miic(), scripts/benchmarks/compare_outputs.R, notebook case2/10):

  • “identical”: same retained links, orientations, genuine causations and values. Not possible against the server: its edge list stores the values rounded to 6 decimals.
  • “same decisions, values differ”: same links, orientations and genuine causations; the best possible verdict against the server. Expect the confidence column to differ even with the same settings: the server’s random seed for the permutations is not ours (2026). On our inputs this never changed a decision (checked on the authors’ case study 2 job: same 715 links, 62 confidence values differ, by at most 0.008).
  • “different network”: look at the settings first (step 1), then at the input (step 2). The links that differ:
reference_run <- local_server_settings_run %||% local_run
if (!is.null(reference_run)) {
  both <- full_join(miic_links(server_result) |> filter(type == "P"), miic_links(reference_run) |> filter(type == "P"),
                    by = "link", suffix = c("_server", "_local"))
  list(only_server  = both |> filter(is.na(type_local)) |> select(link, info_shifted_server, confidence_server),
       only_local   = both |> filter(is.na(type_server)) |> select(link, info_shifted_local, confidence_local),
       orientation  = both |> filter(orientation_server != orientation_local | is_causal_server != is_causal_local) |>
                        select(link, orientation_server, orientation_local, is_causal_server, is_causal_local)) |>
    map(\(t) head(t, 10))
}

9. Reading the network

The edge list (all.edges.summary) has one row per pair of variables examined. The columns that matter:

Column Meaning
type P = retained link; N = removed
info_shifted strength of the link (MI × number of cells, minus the complexity cost)
infOrt 1 = not oriented, 2 = x → y, -2 = y → x, 6 = bidirected (latent common cause)
is_causal Y = genuine causation: the arrow is supported by a downstream v-structure, not only by an arrowhead
proba arrowhead probabilities, written “x-side;y-side” (the opposite of the documentation)
confidence confidence ratio from the permutations (lower = more confident)

Two artefacts of the causalccc branch of miic:

  • L-R placeholder rows. Each L-R pair appears twice: a placeholder (strength 0, Nxy_ai = 0) and the imposed link. retained_links() drops the placeholders (Nxy_ai %in% 0: use %in%, not ==, because of NA).
  • L-R strengths are not measured. Every L-R link gets the strength of the strongest link of the network:
reference <- runs[["authors' settings (reference)"]]
ref_links <- retained_links(reference, small_edges)
ref_links |> filter(is_lr) |> select(x, y, info_shifted)
# A tibble: 4 × 3
  x      y     info_shifted
  <chr>  <chr>        <dbl>
1 MIF    CD74         2562.
2 MIF    CD44         2562.
3 MIF    CXCR4        2562.
4 CXCL12 CXCR4        2562.
max(ref_links$info_shifted[!ref_links$is_lr])
[1] 2561.709

“Upstream” and “downstream” in the paper mean the position relative to the L-R link (sender side, receiver side), not a direction found by MIIC: links next to the receptor are often unoriented.

The neighbourhood of the L-R pairs (diamonds), two links deep:

plot_neighbourhood(reference$all.edges.summary |> filter(!(link_name(x, y) %in% ref_links$link[ref_links$is_lr] & Nxy_ai %in% 0)),
                   lr_links = ref_links$link[ref_links$is_lr],
                   centres  = unique(c(small_edges$ligand, small_edges$receptor)),
                   cell_type_of = side_of,
                   label_of = \(v) str_remove(v, "_(senders|receivers)$"),
                   max_distance = 2, title = "Fibroblasts → DCs, around CXCL12/MIF and CXCR4/CD74/CD44")

The direct neighbours of CXCL12 and CXCR4 (direction seen from the centre: out = centre → neighbour):

intracellular <- ref_links |> filter(!is_lr)
bind_rows(neighbors_of("CXCL12", intracellular), neighbors_of("CXCR4", intracellular)) |>
  select(node, neighbor, direction, is_causal) |>
  knitr::kable()
node neighbor direction is_causal
CXCL12 CXCL14 none N
CXCL12 labels_senders out N
CXCL12 CFH none N
CXCL12 CFD out N
CXCL12 IFITM3 none N
CXCR4 RGS1 none N
CXCR4 NR4A3 none N
CXCR4 HLA-B none N

Even on this 51-variable network, CXCL12 is linked to CXCL14, CFH and CFD (oriented CXCL12 → CFD), and CXCR4 to RGS1 and NR4A3: the neighbours the paper names for Figure 3 (notebook case2/03).

CXCL12 also points to labels_senders, the fibroblast subtype. An arrow from a gene to a metadata variable is not a biological statement: CXCL12 is a marker of a subtype. Metadata that genes cannot cause (condition, patient, batch) can be declared contextual in the state order (is_contextual = 1), so that MIIC never orients links towards them. The published case studies did not do it (all variables have is_contextual = 0).

How much to trust what. From the reproduction of case study 2 (notebooks case2/06 and case2/07): with the same cells and slightly different gene selections, links are robust (Jaccard 0.85–0.92 per cell type), orientations of shared links mostly agree (96 %), but genuine causations are not (8 shared of 14 and 12). Read links first, orientations with care, and treat a single genuine causation as a hypothesis.

10. Checklist

Step Check / setting Why
Raw data integer counts in the counts layer; recover them if only log-normalised values exist (known scale factor) MI is computed on counts
Raw data JoinLayers() after Seurat 5 integration; never SCT, scaled or integrated values the functions read one counts layer
Raw data unique gene names, same annotation as the L-R resource unmatched L-R genes are dropped silently
QC filter empty droplets, damaged cells and doublets per cell type before building the table every cell enters the network
QC detection rate of each L-R gene in its cell type (< 10 % = weak) MI needs variation
Populations enough cells (hundreds), and metadata (condition, subtype, possibly binned library size) for pooled data confounders create links
L-R pairs one table per sender → receiver direction; check the order (cap of 8) the wrapper handles one direction
Selection n_genes from the MI curves and the network size you can afford (~25 per run here) size and run time
Selection more than 8 ligands or receptors: call causalCCC.MIselection() directly the wrapper drops the extra ones silently
Selection remove the metadata from the selected genes; patch the wrapper with two metadata or more a metadata column can be selected as a gene
Selection remove ribosomal / mitochondrial genes from the candidates if they dominate the MI ranking they follow library size
Selection keep the MI tables (save = TRUE) and redo the selection with select_genes() seconds instead of hours
Selection compute the MI tables with compute_mi_table(), blocks of about 100 genes same table, faster, a third of the memory
Mosaic several directions: pool per cell type, name <gene>_<cell type>, check for duplicated columns duplicates make contradictory orientations
Mosaic discrete rule “≤ 5 values counting NA”; set.seed() before building same rules as the package, reproducible order
MIIC interact_edges with columns ligand, receptor; n_threads = 1, or 8 with the patched variant late failure; crashes
MIIC no identical columns (duplicated_columns()) duplicates double links and destabilise orientations
MIIC check result$params: invalid values (cplx = "bic") are replaced by the defaults silent change of settings
MIIC metadata that genes cannot cause: is_contextual = 1 no arrows towards condition or batch
MIIC state the settings: ori_proba_ratio, n_shuffles, conf_threshold (authors: 0.01, 100, 0.01) they change orientations and the number of links
Web server set confidence cut = yes, 100 shuffles, threshold 0.01, orientation probability ratio 0.01; compare the job with a local run (section 8b) the form’s defaults are not the authors’ settings
Reading drop L-R placeholder rows; ignore L-R strengths artefacts of the causalccc branch
Reading trust links > orientations > genuine causations robustness measured in case study 2
